facts.statement: Angulomastacator is a genus of duck-billed dinosaur whose name means "bend chewer".
facts.quote: Angulomastacator (meaning "bend chewer", in reference to both the shape of its upper jaw and to the Big Bend area of the Rio Grande, where the type specimen was found) is a genus of duck-billed dinosaur

facts.statement: The genus is known from a single fossil specimen consisting of a partial left upper jaw bone.
facts.quote: It is known from a single specimen, TxVP 43681–1, a partial left maxilla (the main tooth-bearing bone of the upper jaw).

facts.statement: The fossilized upper jaw bone is curved down by approximately 45 degrees at the front, a feature unique among hadrosaurs.
facts.quote: This bone is curved down approximately 45° at its anterior end, with the tooth row bent to fit, unlike any other hadrosaur.

facts.statement: Angulomastacator belongs to the lambeosaurine group of hadrosaurs, which are characterized by hollow cranial crests.
facts.quote: Angulomastacator is classified as a lambeosaurine, the group of hadrosaurs with hollow cranial crests.

facts.statement: The fossil was found in the upper shale member of the Aguja Formation within deposits interpreted as a small tributary channel.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the upper shale member of the Aguja Formation, among plant, bone, and clam fragments in a bed interpreted as the deposits of a small tributary channel.

facts.statement: A partial maxilla and vertebrae were found in dark grey mudstone, showing signs of transport by water during a flooding event.
facts.quote: J. Browning discovered a partial maxilla and some vertebrae in the dark grey mudstone, with weathering to suggest that they had been transported by water from a disarticulated skeleton during a flooding event.

facts.statement: The species was formally described as the new taxon Angulomastacator daviesi in 2009 by Lehman and Wagner.
facts.quote: Lehman and Jonathan Wagner to describe it as the new taxon Angulomastacator daviesi in 2009.

facts.statement: Angulomastacator lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 77 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 77 millones de años, en el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the unique characteristics of the maxilla support the hypothesis that the dinosaurs of the Aguja Formation were endemic forms.
facts.quote: The unusual characteristics of the maxilla, which have not been reported from elsewhere, supports the hypothesis that the dinosaurs of the Aguja Formation were endemic forms.

facts.statement: Angulomastacator is classified within the family Hadrosauridae, subfamily Lambeosaurinae, and possibly the tribe Lambeosaurini.
facts.quote: familia: Hadrosauridae subfamilia: Lambeosaurinae tribus: Lambeosaurini?

facts.statement: The time range for the genus is recorded as Campanian, spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The fossil locality dates to the middle Campanian, approximately 76.6 million years ago, based on comparison with a nearby pyroclastic flow dated to 76.9 ± 1.2 million years ago.
rejected.quote: This locality is from the upper shale of the Aguja Formation, just below the younger Javelina Formation, of Big Bend, Texas, and is comparable in age to a nearby pyroclastic flow dated to 76.9 ± 1.2 million years ago, suggesting a reasonable middle Campanian age of 76.6 mya.
